content.summary_of_the_paper: This work addresses the problem of improving training and testing efficiency of a previous work on GNN based cross-document misinformation detection by Wu et al. (2022). As the original detector is not compact and uses separate GNN models for document and entity level misinformation detection (the models take over 300MB disk space) and inference is slow, it is claimed that it (and other misinformation detectors in the literature) can't be easily deployed on resource-constrained devices thereby limiting their applicability. The work proposes to overcome the bottlenecks by making use of sparsity mask in GNN training and inference and by using a single GNN for both document and entity level misinformation detection. While the use of sparsity masks is not new for the purposes of improving training and testing efficiency of neural networks, the work argues that sparsity masks in the literature are not hardware-friendly. It proposes a sparsity pattern, CircuSparsity, which is not derived from the base model but is predefined. The proposed sparsity matrix is composed with irreducible patterns of desired level of sparsity and their cyclic shifts. As the pattern is predefined, it enables hardware locality opening up opportunities for speedup. The work proposes another improvement to GNN based cross-document misinformation detection by Wu et al. (2022) - use of a single GNN for both  document and entity level misinformation detection. It uses an early exit strategy where the document level classifier makes use of representations computed by an intermediate layer instead of the final layer. Experimental results demonstrate that with the proposed enhancements, the misinformation detector can do as well as the original at 50-75% sparsity. Datasets used for the experiments are the same as those used in Wu et al. (2022): IED, TL17, and Crisis. Ablation results for the early exit of document classifier, the document-event weight 1’s position in base sparsity pattern are also presented.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
     1. The proposed pre-fixed sparsity pattern is simple and seems to work well. Empirical results are very encouraging.
     

Weaknesses:
    1. The proposed sparsity technique seems to be limited in scope. While it has been shown to work well for a particular misinformation detector, there is no guarantee that it will work well for other networks.
   2. Though the experimental results are encouraging, it is not clear why the simple pre-fixed should work well. No explanation is provided.
  3.  The dataset used for evaluation is not a widely used dataset. Basically only previous work has used it and this work is an extension of the previous work. 
  4. There is no novelty in the methodological aspects of the work.


Questions for the authors:
	1. Why do misinformation detection models need to be deployed on smartphones? Can you give a real-world use case?
	2. How does the proposed sparsity pattern compare with masks that are inferred from a pretrained model or learned during training?
	3. Wu et al use event level detection results for document: "these two tasks are not mutually independent. Intuitively, document-level detection can benefit from the results of event-level detection, because the presence of a large number of false events indicates that the document is more likely to be fake. Therefore, we feed the results produced by a well-trained event-level detector into each layer of the document-level detector." Their ablation study (Table 4) shows that event level detection is crucial for getting best document level results (86.76 vs 84.57 F1). This seems to go against your claim that document level detection model needs to be separated from event level detection model.
	4.  Results in Table 1 (doc classifier exit #4) doesn't match with those of Wu et al. Why is sparse model giving better results than unpruned?
	5. HSF, GROVER and CDMD are fake news detection algorithms whereas MP and LTH are sparse n/w methods. Which fake news detection algorithm is used in conjunction with MP and LTH? (Table 4)
	6. Doc classifier exit #1 is nearly as good as exit # 2. And there's not a whole lot of difference b/w exit #1 and exit #4. Is this because document level event detection is a easy problem or something to do with the dataset?
	7. Why no event level results for 90% sparsity in Table 4? Do the event level results degrade more drastically than even level as the sparsity is increased?
	8. Why no results for a random sparsity pattern? That would be a good baseline for relative assessment of sparsity patterns.
	9. In Tables 4,5  and 6, why is SMD 90% sparsity better than SMD 50%? 
	10. Looks like all sparsity patterns do almost equally well. No insight provided as to what is happening here. Is this something unique to the sparsity detection problem or is this true for GNN in general?

Section 4.3: presentation bits --> representation bits
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The submission is well written and easy to understand. The proposed sparsity pattern is simple and should be easy to reproduce. but not novel. There is not much novelty in methodological aspects and the work is primarily empirical in nature. Experimental study is thorough except for some aspects mentioned in the questions above. The applicability of the proposed approach is limited to one specific misinformation detection work in the literature.
content.summary_of_the_review: This work looks at the problem of improving training and testing efficiency of a particular misinformation detector. It proposes a simple pre-fixed sparsity pattern and demonstrates that this pattern is effective for the aforementioned misinformation detector. It also proposes to use a single GNN model for both document and event level misinformation detection. Several key questions on why the sparsity pattern works for this detector and the applicability of the proposed pattern to other networks is not yet addressed.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a misinformation detector for efficient misinformation detection, which consists of two main designs: CircuSparsity and early exit.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths of the paper:
Well-written and easy to follow.
A number of datasets are applied to evaluate the performance of the proposed model.

Weaknesses of the paper:
The paper suffers from the lack of novelty. The contribution in terms of the graph neural network algorithms is very marginal. The contribution in terms of making the model run faster is also marginal. The main contributions of the paper lie in the design of two main components, CircuSparsity and early exit, which are straightforward.

For some datasets, there are no event information available, making the proposed model limits itself to a specific setting.

The proposed model is built based on Wu’s model. However, it is unclear why the authors aim to build their model based on Wu’s model. There are a large number of misinformation detection models being proposed, either graph-based, even-based or not. Not sure if the authors are able to model the misinformation detection based on other detection models.

There are a large number of papers that extend the standard GCN model. It is unclear why the author didn’t build their own detection model based on state-of-the-art GCN models, such as the following GCN models (just list a few):
Mehta et al., Tackling fake news detection by continually improving social context representations using graph neural networks, in ACL 2022
Fang et al., Structure-aware random fourier kernel for graphs, in NeurIPS 2021

There are a large number of papers that aim at making the GCN models run faster. Not sure why the authors didn’t build their GCN model by extending from the previous efficient GCN models.

content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Strengths

1. The problem is timely
2. The technique gives importance to efficiency, which is often neglected in papers on this topic


# Weaknesses

1. The paper discusses misinfo detection but it looks more like a paper on sparse GNN learning
2. Experiments are not conclusive as results are often not "statistically significant"
3. The paper is difficult to read and sometimes it is difficult to understand the techniques explaned.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is not clear and difficult to understant. The novelty is also questionable, although, in this case it is clear that the main novelty should come from the techniques used in the experiments. The idea of using sparse GNN for this task is novel enough. The quality of experiments are not enough for the level of quality required for a top conference like ICLR.
content.summary_of_the_review:
I have the following questions to authors:

1. Why do you consider this as a Misinfo detection paper when you do not test the method against any of the known datasets for misinfo? Take TL17 dataset. As far as I know this has been algorithmically built out of a dataset of real news that are manipulated to build some fake news. In particular it is not so clear that for every fake news you have a certain amount of corresponding valid news. This might, indeed, impair the actual effectiveness of your method on real news. All in all, the paper looks more like a paper on sparsity learning on graphs, rather than misinfo detection; see Table 4, for instance.

2. The paper contains some statements which are not really corresponding to any experiments corroborating the statement, or they are not well explained. For example:
      * "However, this naive way does not work well. As we will show in the experiments, the two losses are actually against each other. Combining them together often degrades the performance of document and event misinformation detection (compared to using a separate GNN for each task exclusively)."
      * "GNN itself is pretty redundant"
      * "most irreducible pattern". What is that? How do you define most irreducible?

3. Why CircuSparsity is superior?

4. No difference in results is statistically significant. If you look at results all the confidence intervals overlap, somehow. How can you decide which method is best?

content.title: Sparse Misinformation Detector
content.abstract: We present Sparse Misinformation Detector (SMD), a new efficient misinformation detection network with regular fine-grained sparsity. We propose two technical components to enable SMD. First, CircuSparsity, a new hardware-friendly sparsity pattern, is introduced for improved training and testing efficiency. Second, through dedicated empirical analyses, we discover that document-level misinformation detection is pretty insensitive to a compact model size, which inspires us to make early exit for the document-level misinformation classifier. With these two techniques, we successfully achieve efficient misinformation detection on both document and event levels with one single model. Empirically, our approach significantly outperforms the original dense misinformation detection network while enjoying 50% to 75% sparsity. Extensive experiments and analyses demonstrate the merits of our method compared to other top-performing counterpart approaches. To our best knowledge, this is the first attempt for efficient misinformation detection from the network sparse training perspective.
